newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices recover as refinery margins improve.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices recover as refinery margins improve.

text.p: Oil prices recovered from early losses on Thursday as stronger U.S. markets for gasoline and heating oil lifted profit margins for refiners, dealers said.

International benchmark Brent Blend crude futures for April delivery closed 30 cents firmer at $19.70 a barrel on London's International Petroleum Exchange after dipping early to $19.16 under the weight of rising crude supply in what is usually a slack season for oil demand.
"U.S. gasoline led the way this afternoon," said a broker.
"It has come out of hibernation and that seems to be what's rattling the market, although there's also some talk of colder weather returning to the U.S. Northeast," he added.

Private forecaster Weather Services Corp (WSC) said temperatures in the region would average five degrees Fahrenheit below normal on Friday and stay low througout the weekend, stoking demand for heating oil fuel.
Dealers said April gasoline prices on New York's Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) were nearing three-week highs, helped by signs of falling inventories ahead of the key summer driving season.
On Wednesday, the U.S. Department of Energy said gasoline stocks fell by 2.3 million barrels last week.

Despite the modest recovery, Brent is still more than $5 a barrel below this year's high, depressed by the return of Iraqi exports, combined with increased production by members of the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC).

"The full impact of this supply surge (of Iraqi oil) will be felt heavily this spring, and will continue to weigh down prices," said an oil market report by Washington-based industry consultants Petroleum Finance Company.

Exports under the United Nations' oil-for-food deal have crept higher in recent weeks as spot sales over and above original sales contracts have been sanctioned by the U.N. in an effort to make up for a shortfall in revenues.
Baghdad is allowed to sell oil to the value of $1 billion in the 90 days to March and another $1 billion worth by June 9.
But Iraq's State Oil Marketing Organisation (SOMO) and customers are struggling to find homes for cargoes in the well-supplied markets of the United States, Europe and the Far East.
Adding to downward pressure was a report on Thursday that OPEC producers kept their foot on the accelerator in February, pumping 130,000 barrels per day (bpd) more crude than the previous month.

Production reached 26.77 million barrels per day in February, over 1.7 million bpd above the official output quota of 25.033 million bpd for the 11-member cartel, a survey by Reuters of OPEC officials, oil companies and analysts found.

"When the market was able to absorb everything thrown at it, it didn't matter. But if prices come off much more then OPEC overproduction will become an issue for the market again," said an OPEC member country official.

Annual refinery maintenance is stifling demand at many plants in the United States and Europe, while some poor profit margins for European refineries have forced many to reduce their output, thus cutting back on the crude they need to run.

"There is a general feeling that most nearby requirements are covered both sides of the Atlantic, with upcoming (refinery) maintenance programmes reducing demand. Supplies however are expected to remain ample," said Lawrence Eagles of commodity brokers GNI in a daily report on Thursday.
And when the maintenance season in Europe and the United States in over, Asian refiners will be ready to spruce up their own plants.
"Refinery maintenance has started trimming crude demand in the Atlantic Basin, and will be moving to Asia in the second quarter," said Petroleum Finance Company in their report.
